When Rachel Maniscalco was placed on unpaid leave from her teaching job at Concord High School on Staten Island in October 2021, she almost lost everything along with it. Her husband earned too much money working at JFK International Airport to qualify for food stamps but not enough to support the whole family. The bills quickly started piling up: the mortgage, utilities, car insurance. And because Maniscalco’s older daughter had medical issues, the family had to start paying $600 a month for private health insurance. Maniscalco drained her retirement savings; her husband drained his savings.

To try and make ends meet, Maniscalco started working at a tax office and picking up night shifts at a bar, along with other side gigs—anything to patch together an income. One hundred dollars from the bar would be enough to cover a few weeknight dinners; a fifty-dollar tutoring session would buy two cans of formula for her newborn. Between all the odd jobs, Maniscalco barely got any sleep. “I was running on fumes for years,” she told me. Still, it wasn’t enough: “Things are going to be scarce . . . for a little bit,” she recalls telling her daughter.

Why did Maniscalco—a special education and English teacher in New York City public schools for over a decade—lose her job? She was one of the thousands of educators, police officers, sanitation workers, and other city employees who refused to get the Covid-19 vaccine. Maniscalco didn’t know this when she first lost her job, but she would help start a movement that would unite thousands of aggrieved citizens in opposition to New York’s immunization requirements for public workers. The “reinstate and compensate” movement, as it is sometimes referred to by its devotees, is a microcosm of the libertarian approach to public health that has been galvanized nationwide since the pandemic.

Though New York City eventually jettisoned its mandate and allowed most unvaccinated workers to return to their jobs, Maniscalco and many others like her are not back at work—they’re still fighting for the cause of “medical freedom.” Indeed, they’ve been welcomed with open arms into the Make America Healthy Again coalition against government authority and elite expertise in most every form, public health be damned.

Before Covid, Maniscalco never cared much about politics. “I lived my life very focused on how I’m getting through . . . the next paycheck cycle,” she told me. But then normal life ground to a halt: In March 2020, Maniscalco and her family were suddenly stuck together in the house all day. Maniscalco sat at the dining room table every morning and tried to work with her students over Zoom—but it was a struggle. Her daughter, who was in the third grade at the time, likewise had trouble with remote learning. “I mean, who wouldn’t, really, right? . . . It was just an absolute nightmare.” As the pandemic wore on, Maniscalco grew tired of all the rules, the fear, the doom and gloom. She wanted to focus on the bright side: the doctors who projected that we had a high chance—99.7 percent, as she recalls—of getting through the pandemic. The ones who said you would be just fine as long as you weren’t morbidly obese, old, or had any other comorbidities. That the danger of Covid-19 was wildly overblown.

The reinstate-and-compensate movement “spread like wildfire” through word of mouth and social media.

One of these “doctors” is the decertified Peter McCullough, an early proponent of antiparasitic medications like ivermectin and chloroquine as treatments for Covid-19. McCullough also pushed the narrative that Covid-19 survivors had immunity and didn’t need to be vaccinated: “People who develop Covid have complete and durable immunity,” he said in his testimony to the Texas Senate Health and Human Services Committee. “There is no scientific, clinical, or safety rationale for ever vaccinating a Covid-recovered patient.” His ideas were circulated by manosphere conspiracists like Joe Rogan, who parroted McCullough’s unsubstantiated claims to millions, even alleging he had treated himself with ivermectin.

Maniscalco, along with millions of others, was swept up in this cataclysmic information battle that politicized what, for most, was a public health emergency requiring a nonpartisan response. As she researched further, Maniscalco grew increasingly skeptical of the vaccine, which became widely available to New Yorkers in April 2021. “I read one study from the New England Journal of Medicine that said that [the vaccine] was not definitively safe for pregnant women,” she told me. She appeared to be referring to a study published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in April 2021, which concluded that “preliminary findings did not show obvious safety signals among pregnant persons who received mRNA Covid-19 vaccines.” The term “safety signal” is pharmaceutical regulation jargon for “information on a new or known adverse event that is potentially caused by a medicine and that warrants further investigation,” meaning that, in actuality, the CDC’s conclusion was that there was no evidence of unexpected safety problems for pregnant people in its preliminary trial.

Maniscalco came to believe that the vaccine was foisted onto the public to generate profits for its manufacturers. “If you look at it from a financial perspective, people made so much money off of this experimental pharmaceutical,” she contended. “Big Pharma controls so much—including the media, by the way, all of the media—that the only thing that made sense to me was that the kickbacks were so monumental that no one could go against this Goliath.”

The conviction that federal agencies bolster pharmaceutical companies’ profits is, of course, not without a basis in reality. Between 2014 and 2018, the CDC accepted close to $80 million from drug companies and other corporations through its charitable foundation. The federal government, in turn, poured approximately $18 billion into accelerating vaccine research and development through Operation Warp Speed. But despite taxpayers already bankrolling much of the vaccine effort, the U.S. government paid Pfizer about $1.95 billion for the first 100 million doses and later paid Moderna about $3.3 billion for an additional 200 million doses. In 2022—just one year after governments around the world began distributing Covid vaccines—Pfizer’s revenue hit $100 billion, a new record. A few months later, both Pfizer and Moderna quadrupled the price of their vaccines.

In August 2021, Maniscalco learned that New York City would require her to receive at least one dose of the vaccine to return to in-person work—or else be placed on unpaid leave. She knew she wasn’t going to comply. She had just had her second daughter in June at thirty-six years old, and the fear of any possible complications about having a baby at her age led her to increased skepticism about the vaccine. She decided that she would not put “anything in my body that may lead to a negative outcome.” Other employees told me they refused the vaccine due to their religious beliefs. One former public school social worker told me she did not get the vaccine because she is a pro-life Catholic and had read that the vaccine was created using “abortion cells.” But since 2019, New York has been one of only five states that do not allow religious or personal exemptions from school vaccine requirements.

On October 4, the first day of school after the mandates took effect, Maniscalco was one of eight thousand employees who were unable to work because they refused the vaccine. And that was just the Department of Education. A month later, another nine thousand employees from the fire, police, and sanitation departments were placed on unpaid leave.

It was around that time that Maniscalco started a new Instagram account dedicated to protesting the vaccine mandate. One of Maniscalco’s first posts is a video of her standing at a microphone at a protest in Manhattan. Her hair is in a ponytail, and her newborn bounces in her arms as her voice reverberates through the industrial speakers. She tells the assembled crowd that she’s been reaching out to the teachers’ union, asking it to support their decision not to get vaccinated, but that it had not responded. She says that PCR tests are “bullshit” and that the powers that be “don’t care about medical freedom and bodily autonomy.” (Today, the account boasts around seventeen thousand followers.)

According to Maniscalco, the reinstate and compensate movement “spread like wildfire” through word of mouth and social media. That’s how she met Michael Kane, a former high school teacher in Queens who shared her grievances and her outspokenness. After the mandate was announced, Kane established Teachers for Choice, an organization that shares vaccine-related news and updates at the federal and state levels. Its ethos is simple: As Kane put it on his Substack, the movement opposes all “forced medical mandates for any American to access society or keep their job.”

Kane and Maniscalco ramped up their efforts to lobby the teachers’ union to stand up to NYC Public Schools (NYCPS), then known as the NYC Department of Education, on their behalf. The United Federation of Teachers (UFT) was generally supportive of vaccination programs for teachers in New York City, but it did make some effort to advocate for the anti-vaccination teachers. The UFT negotiated for teachers with medical exemptions to teach remotely, health benefits for teachers placed on leave, and severance options for those who would not comply. Nevertheless, in August 2021, Kane posted a press release to announce he was leaving the union. “The UFT is no longer a union. What union in history has ever actively worked to have their members placed on unpaid leave or fired?” Kane wrote on his Substack. “This is one of the saddest days of my life.”

David C. Bloomfield, a professor of education law at Brooklyn College and the CUNY Graduate Center, is sympathetic to the position the UFT took during the pandemic. “The UFT had members who may have wanted [to be] protected from other members,” he mused. “So, I think the UFT was put in a spot.” A spokesperson for the UFT said that the union worked with NYCPS to help its members seek religious and medical exemptions. Maniscalco remembers it differently: “Our union, who I paid dues to for a decade, did absolutely nothing for us. . . . You go against what they want, what the city wants, what the union wants, what the union signs up for, [and] they will fuck you every which way.”

Of the over sixteen thousand municipal employees who were placed on unpaid leave around the time the mandate went into effect, most caved within a few days. By November 10, 2021, only 2,600 New York City employees remained on unpaid leave. By 2022, the city started firing the holdouts. Maniscalco and Kane were two of nearly 1,000 NYCPS employees and over 1,700 municipal employees who were terminated during these sweeping layoffs.

Maniscalco, Kane, and hundreds of other fired workers subsequently turned to the courts. Maniscalco hired a lawyer. Jimmy Wagner—whose wife was also a teacher wary of the vaccine at the time—took on her case and several other tenured teachers’ cases pro bono at first. Wagner argues that Maniscalco’s firing was not only unjustified but also illegal because she had tenure. A teacher seeking tenure with NYCPS must complete a four-year probationary period, receive a recommendation from their principal, and have a clean record. If the superintendent grants tenure, the teacher cannot be fired without due process and is entitled to a hearing should NYCPS pursue disciplinary action. “If Rachel Maniscalco had slapped a child . . . she would never have been fired,” Wagner insists.

According to him, New York’s tenure law should have superseded the city’s collective bargaining agreement with the teachers’ union requiring vaccines. He wasn’t arguing that teachers could not be fired—just that they had a right to a hearing and due process, which Maniscalco was denied. Wagner and Maniscalco brought their case to the Supreme Court of New York in March 2022 and again in February 2023. Both times, they lost.

For its part, NYCPS argued that due process was not violated because their placement on leave was “unrelated to job performance, misconduct or competency” and therefore didn’t count as disciplinary action. “Tenure protections aren’t built for the situation that the city found itself in in 2020,” said Dr. Bloomfield. He allows that the tenure statute in New York education law is “procedurally complex and drawn-out,” but even so, he remains “dubious about its applicability in this situation.”

And then a funny thing happened: In February 2023, New York City lifted the vaccine mandate for municipal workers. But within the NYCPS, fired employees were not immediately reinstated to their posts; they had to reapply for them. During this process, many, including Maniscalco, discovered that their personnel files had been flagged with “problem codes,” delaying their background checks. Maniscalco, Kane, and a group of others testified in a city council hearing in December 2023 to have these removed—to no avail.

In the years since, Maniscalco, Kane, and other rising figures in the anti-vaccination space have pressed ahead, testifying at city council hearings, appearing in court proceedings, and lobbying politicians. In February 2025, Maniscalco and her lawyer founded a new political organization: the Donald J. Trump Kings County Republican Club. Originally, it was dedicated to electing local politicians whose politics aligned with the reinstate and compensate movement, but after disappointing results in that year’s election, the club pivoted to reforming the city charter.

The first two proposed changes are to allow elected officials to be recalled and to create an elected Office of Municipal Worker Fairness. From Wagner’s point of view, this is all about freedom: the ever-contentious, all-important American right to choose. “For the last sixty years, all women in New York State have heard is ‘my body, my choice.’ How, in the blink of an eye, [do] they go from ‘my body, my choice’ to the government’s choice?”

Maniscalco and Wagner now insist that their movement is ultimately about workers’ rights.

While Wagner, Maniscalco, and other vocal advocates of the “reinstate and compensate” movement have stressed to me time and time again that they are not MAGA acolytes, they are animated by hostility to the Democratic Party, which they see as responsible for the economic hardship they have endured in recent years. Bill de Blasio created the mandate, but it was during the Eric Adams administration that NYCPS employees were officially terminated en masse. In the eyes of fired workers, Adams had not only ignored their grievances but underscored them when, in the spring of 2022, he lifted the vaccine mandate for athletes and performers but not city workers. By the time the mandate for city workers was finally lifted a year later, it was seen by many as too little, too late.

On the morning of November 5, 2025—less than twenty-four hours after Zohran Mamdani won the mayoral election—the lame-duck Adams administration announced that the city’s administrative department, the Department of Citywide Administrative Services (DCAS), would hold a public hearing for the proposed “Reinstatement of Employees Dismissed for Noncompliance with the COVID-19 Vaccination Mandate.” If approved, this rule would have allowed 2,900 former city workers to reapply for their old titles at their former salaries—but without backpay. Despite a flurry of excitement at the end of the year, the proposal was never voted on and was lost in a bureaucratic abyss. (DCAS did not respond to multiple requests for comment.)

When Mamdani stepped into the mayor’s office on January 1, I assumed that Maniscalco and her fellow activists would be enraged by the election of a self-proclaimed socialist—after all, I had heard them decry the city’s progressives as “violent oligarchs” and the “radical left” more than once. But when asked about the new administration, Maniscalco appeared wary, but not close-minded. Throughout his campaign, Mamdani centered his platform around making life in New York City easier for the working class. But what remains to be seen, in Maniscalco’s eyes, is whether his pro-worker ethos will extend across ideological lines. “Is it every worker,” she wonders, “or the people you agree with?”

Last March on the campaign trail, movement organizers reported that Mamdani “seemed genuinely interested” when they handed him a flyer outlining their grievances. Allegedly, he told them that he did not want them to “fall through the cracks.” But about a month later, Mamdani backtracked while speaking with former New York Police Department lieutenant John Macari on his podcast New York’s Finest: Retired and Unfiltered. A listener and NYPD officer named Marlon, who was fired for refusing the vaccine, submitted a question: If elected mayor, would Mamdani hire him back to the force? Mamdani sympathized with Marlon and acknowledged that some of the city’s pandemic-era rules had been arbitrary. But he also stressed the importance of following public health guidance during an emergency like the pandemic. “Ultimately, if you asked me today, would I be hiring Marlon back? I think I would fall on the side of no because of the concerns around the necessity of upholding that public health mandate.” (The mayor’s office did not respond to a request for comment.)

On a freezing Tuesday morning this past March, Maniscalco and other reinstate and compensate activists woke up at the crack of dawn to take a bus to the New York State Capitol in Albany for “Vaccine Rights Advocacy Day”— an annual rally in Empire State Plaza. At the rally, people held up homemade signs plastered with Health and Human Services Secretary John Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.’s smiling face and messages like “COERCION ≠ CONSENT.” Michael Kane was the event’s emcee. As he stepped into the center of the crowd, he began a chant: “Hands off our children.” Behind him, a three-drum, one-trombone band accompanied the crowd’s fervent cheers.

Someone gave me a flyer that was printed on both sides with horrifying statistics like “40 percent of all kids have a vaccine-induced chronic illness” (presumably, this came from the White House’s 2025 MAHA Report, which lists the percentage but never attributes it to vaccines). There were screenshots of blurry tables and graphs from medical studies (cited but easily discredited after even a cursory skim of authoritative sources). At the bottom of the page, Children’s Health Defense’s website was printed in big, bold lettering.

CHD—a nonprofit organization founded in 2007 by Eric Gladen as the World Mercury Project—was the main sponsor of the rally; its banner hung behind Kane as he spoke (Kane also recently became CHD’s Director of Advocacy). Children’s Health Defense is a MAHA-backed nonprofit that uses incessant litigation to advance legislation that rolls back vaccine requirements and other perceived threats to “medical freedom.” The group rose to prominence in 2015 when it appointed a new chairman and chief general counsel: Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. Appropriately, one of Children’s Health Defense’s central functions is to engage in endless litigation.

In New York City, CHD’s legal arm has represented several fired workers in wrongful termination lawsuits. Kane was represented by CHD attorney Sujata Gibson in his lawsuit against the city. Although Kane’s case was dismissed by the U.S. Supreme Court after five years of appeals and petitions, the Supreme Court also recently directed a lower court to review New York’s statewide ban on religious exemptions. CHD’s attorneys are persistent, and not without good reason. A couple of fired workers in the sanitation and fire departments achieved reinstatement through legal challenges and accommodation requests, and in October 2022, sixteen sanitation workers won reinstatement and back pay after a Staten Island court called the vaccine mandate itself arbitrary and capricious. Wagner himself told me that some of his clients had successfully sued for reinstatement and backpay. He told me he had “no theory” as to why Maniscalco’s lawsuits had failed while others hadn’t. “It’s the luck of the draw.”

CHD CEO Mary Holland was the final speaker at the Albany rally. She announced she and Gibson had filed a new suit against the state to restore religious exemptions from vaccination for children attending New York schools. This is just one of their several active lawsuits across the country, and they are not alone: in January, CHD and a dozen or so adjacent organizations announced they had signed on to the Medical Freedom Act Coalition, which has lobbied for state-level bills that loosen public health regulations and mandates. (The coalition’s motto is: “No one and no government has the right to mandate medical interventions.”) They have already successfully passed legislation in Idaho that “prevents schools, businesses, and day cares from mandating medical interventions” at all. In February, Iowa advanced a bill to eliminate school vaccine requirements entirely.

The coalition is working with at least four other states across the country to advance similar bills. As of this June, Florida’s campaign to end school vaccine mandates had stalled, while Arizona’s governor vetoed bills that would have banned mask mandates and loosened vaccine requirements. Still, dozens of anti-vaccine or exemption-expanding bills are active in legislatures across the country. The Trump administration is also pushing for reinstatements of laid off or fired workers at the federal level—in January 2025, Trump directed the Department of Defense to reinstate all service members dismissed for vaccine noncompliance. Since then, approximately two hundred troops and eighty-five Coast Guard members have been reinstated.

However, after a series of CDC and FDA decisions that seemed to favor vaccines, fired workers have started to wonder whether the Trump administration is truly on their side. The New York Times ran two feature stories in the spring about the fracturing of the MAHA–MAGA alliance. Although RFK, Jr.’s initial actions seemed promising, courts, Congress, and internal HHS pressure have reversed or stymied much of the MAHA agenda. Derrick Wynne, a MAHA adherent who was discharged from the Army for refusing a Covid vaccine, told the Times that he now believes Kennedy “was using our movement to gain a huge amount of traction.”

At this point, Maniscalco doesn’t even want her job back at NYCPS. “Could I go back and feel at peace? Could I feel safe? Never. I will never feel safe again there. Quite frankly, I don’t know that I’ll ever feel safe in a job again.” For her and other former government workers, the issue is now bigger than their own reinstatement: It’s become a righteous battle for justice. Indeed, Maniscalco and Wagner now insist that their movement is ultimately about workers’ rights. “That’s bipartisan,” Maniscalco told me.

The version of freedom they purport to defend conceives only of individual autonomy—and treats mutual obligation as akin to tyranny. But diseases do not care about our personal freedoms, political leanings, or whether we trust the powers that be. What we have learned through the pandemic is that when we live in community with others, the limits of our bodies do not start or end where they seem to; our bodies are not borders. Whether the vaccine mandates were punitive or arbitrary is no longer the essential question. The question is whether we can rebuild a public health system based on collective responsibility and trust before the next pandemic.
